0.0.n: Introduces the next point in the explanation.

0.1.n: Combines with つ and 目 to make 1つ目, the first item.

0.2.n: A general counting ending; 1つ counts one thing.

0.3.n: Added after a count to show position in a sequence.

0.5.n: ローマ字 means writing Japanese using the Latin alphabet.

0.6.n: Marks the writing system used as a study tool.

0.7.n: 勉強する becomes 勉強しないで to ask someone not to do it.

1.0.n: Refers to Japanese written using the Latin alphabet.

1.1.n: Marks the means used for studying.

1.3.n: Shows that 日本語 is what someone studies.

1.4.n: The て-form of 勉強する connects studying with the description that follows.

1.6.n: Names the language in which someone is skilled.

1.7.n: With 上手, が marks the skill or activity someone is good at.

1.9.n: Links 上手 to 人 so the description directly modifies the person.

1.10.n: The preceding description identifies what kind of person the speaker means.

1.11.n: Makes people fitting that description the topic of the negative statement.

1.12.n: Here もう adds conversational emphasis rather than indicating that something has already happened.

1.13.n: The past form of 見る combines with こと to describe an experience.

1.14.n: After a past-form verb, こと lets the speaker talk about having that experience.

1.15.n: ことないです denies having an experience; conversational Japanese often drops が after こと.

2.0.n: Adds insistence to the advice rather than a literal time meaning.

2.1.n: Makes the instruction firm and emphatic.

2.2.n: This is the beginning of ひらがな, incorrectly split here; it is not a separate word.

2.3.n: This が belongs inside ひらがな and is not a particle.

2.4.n: This な completes ひらがな, the name of a Japanese writing system.

2.5.n: Marks ひらがな as what the listener should memorize.

2.6.n: The て-form of 覚える connects memorizing with the following request to study.

2.8.n: This is the beginning of the second ひらがな, not a separate word.

2.9.n: This が is inside the word ひらがな, not a subject marker.

2.10.n: This segment contains the end of ひらがな plus で, meaning using; it is not the verb なでる.

2.11.n: 勉強する in て-form plus ください makes a polite request.

3.0.n: A casual variant of めんどうくさい, describing something bothersome or tedious.

3.1.n: Turns the description めんどくさい into something the speaker can say they understand.

3.2.n: Marks the bothersome aspect as the topic, setting up a contrast with the advice.

3.3.n: The plain present form expresses understanding; the speaker is implied.

3.4.n: Acknowledges the difficulty before introducing a contrasting warning.

3.6.n: Names the writing system used for the examples that follow.

3.7.n: Marks the writing system used to write the quoted words.

3.9.n: A Latin-letter rendering of ありがとう, quoted as an example rather than used to thank someone.

3.11.n: Lists an example without suggesting the list is complete.

3.13.n: A Latin-letter rendering of こんにちは, quoted as another example.

3.15.n: A casual alternative to と that marks what someone writes here.

3.16.n: 書いている describes ongoing writing; changing いる to いたら makes it an if-condition.

3.18.n: Adds emphasis to the warning rather than referring literally to time.

3.19.n: Paired with a negative verb, it stresses that improvement will not happen.

3.20.n: 成長する becomes negative 成長しない; です adds politeness to the prediction.

3.21.n: Emphasizes the warning as information the listener should take seriously.

0.lit: Well then, first item. Don't study using Roman letters.
0.tip: A verb ending in ないで can be a direct request not to do something.

1.lit: People who study Japanese using Roman letters and are good at Japanese—I really have never seen.
1.tip: A past-form verb plus ことないです means the speaker has never had that experience.

2.lit: Just definitely memorize hiragana, and please study using hiragana.
2.tip: Read ひらがな as one word despite the splits; the following で means using.

3.lit: I understand it's bothersome, but if you keep writing things like Arigato or Konnichiwa in Roman letters, you'll definitely not improve.
3.tip: 書いていたら sets up an if-condition about continuing to write that way, not necessarily about the past.
